subject: dbms
name: Database Management System
exam: TU assessment: 60% final examination set by the university, 40% internal (assignments, lab work, attendance).

units.title: Introduction to DBMS
topics: Why not plain files? Objectives of a DBMS
Seeing the ideas: pictures, figures and the eight-point lists

sections.title: Why not plain files? Objectives of a DBMS
Seeing the ideas: pictures, figures and the eight-point lists

summary: A DBMS manages a database for many users with consistency, security and recovery.
It replaces the redundancy, isolation and integrity problems of file processing.
Costs are money, complexity and overhead; benefits grow with data size and number of users.

units.title: Database Design, Architecture and Model
topics: The design process and the view of data
Structure of a DBMS and three-level architecture
Converting an E-R diagram to tables
Seeing the ideas: views, models and diagrams

sections.title: The design process and the view of data
Structure of a DBMS and three-level architecture
Converting an E-R diagram to tables
Seeing the ideas: views, models and diagrams

summary: Design goes requirements → E-R → relations → physical.
The three-level architecture gives data independence.
E-R models entities, attributes, relationships, cardinality and participation; extended E-R adds ISA and aggregation.
Conversion rules turn the diagram into relational tables mechanically.

units.title: Relational Database Model
topics: Seeing the ideas: tables, keys and queries

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: tables, keys and queries

summary: A relation is a set of unique tuples over atomic domains; keys identify tuples and link tables.
Integrity rules keep data valid across tables.
Relational algebra composes select, project, product, set operations and joins to express any query; outer joins preserve unmatched rows.

units.title: Database Normalization
topics: Seeing the ideas: anomalies, dependencies and decomposition

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: anomalies, dependencies and decomposition

summary: Anomalies come from redundancy; normalization removes it by decomposition.
Closures of attribute sets find keys.
1NF (atomic) → 2NF (no partial) → 3NF (no transitive) → BCNF (all determinants keys) → 4NF (no MVD).

units.title: Creating and Altering Database and Tables (SQL)
topics: Seeing the ideas: constraints in action
Seeing the ideas with photographs: SQL, storage and removal

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: constraints in action
Seeing the ideas with photographs: SQL, storage and removal

summary: SQL is declarative; DDL defines the schema, and constraints enforce integrity inside the database.
Rejected statements show each constraint working; defaults supply missing values.
ALTER evolves a table without data loss; DROP and TRUNCATE differ in how much they remove.

units.title: Manipulating and Querying Data
topics: ORDER BY, aggregates, GROUP BY and HAVING
Seeing the ideas: how a query is really read

sections.title: ORDER BY, aggregates, GROUP BY and HAVING
Seeing the ideas: how a query is really read

summary: SELECT filters, sorts, groups and aggregates; joins combine tables; subqueries nest one query in another.
NULL needs special handling in comparisons and NOT IN.
UPDATE and DELETE change data and need careful WHERE clauses.
Views give named, reusable, controlled windows onto the data.

units.title: Stored Procedures, DML Triggers and Indexing
topics: Seeing the ideas: why indexes, procedures and triggers matter

sections.title: Seeing the ideas: why indexes, procedures and triggers matter

summary: Stored procedures package logic server-side with parameters, defaults, outputs and transaction control; savepoints allow partial rollback.
Triggers react to data changes for audit and validation, with caveats about multi-row events, hidden logic and cost.
Indexes (primary, secondary, dense, sparse, B+ tree, hash, composite) trade space and write speed for read speed.

units.title: Query Processing and Security
topics: The database administrator and security issues
Access protection, user accounts and audits
Seeing the ideas: plans, costs and defences

sections.title: The database administrator and security issues
Access protection, user accounts and audits
Seeing the ideas: plans, costs and defences

summary: The optimiser picks a plan by estimated block transfers; join algorithm choice changes cost by orders of magnitude.
Heuristics (push selections and projections down) and cost-based search find good plans.
The DBA secures the database through accounts, roles, least privilege, audit trails and backups.
DAC lets owners share; MAC enforces classification; encryption protects data at rest and in transit; parameterised queries stop injection.

units.title: Transaction and Concurrency Control
topics: Transaction concept and the simple transaction model
Seeing the ideas: transactions, schedules and locks

sections.title: Transaction concept and the simple transaction model
Seeing the ideas: transactions, schedules and locks

summary: Transactions give ACID; logging provides atomicity and durability.
Isolation levels and serializability define what concurrent execution may look like; acyclic precedence graphs prove correctness.
Locking (2PL, strict 2PL), deadlock handling, multiple granularity and timestamps are the standard concurrency-control tools.
